newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN SAYS EL NINO TAKING TOLL IN ASIA, S. AMERICA.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN SAYS EL NINO TAKING TOLL IN ASIA, S. AMERICA.

text.p: The weather pattern known as El Nino is causing widespread drought in Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines and a heatwave in Venezuela and other places in Latin America, Japan's Meteorological Agency said on Thursday.
"These droughts and heatwaves may continue as long as El Nino continues," said the agency's monthly report on global climate observation for July, issued on Thursday.
The agency said the average water temperature of the central and eastern Pacific on the equatorial belt in July was some 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 Fahrenheit) higher than the norm.

El Nino, meaning the Child Jesus, was a name originally given to the phenomenon for warm water temperatures around Christmas by Peruvian fishermen and was later associated with abnormal weather around the world.
The agency said it was the 13th El Nino to occur since 1950.

In the report issued on Thursday, the agency said there was a possibility that the El Nino phenomenon could be behind the typhoons which hit Japan twice in June -- an unusual month for the storms to reach Japan -- and a drought in North Korea and northeastern China.
"As for Japan and northeastern Asia, we cannot say that the abnormal weather is not related to El Nino," an official of the agency's Climate Prediction Division said.

The monthly report said devastating floods in east and central Europe were not related to El Nino. Heavy rainfall in Europe was triggered by a high-pressure zone that stood still over Scandinavia and which repeatedly sent cold fronts to the south of it, the agency said.
Commenting on the agency report, Professor Toshio Yamagata of Tokyo University said this year's El Nino could be as strong as in 1982-1983, the worst on record.
"There is a possibility that the current El Nino phenomenon could become larger in scale than the one in 1982-1983," Yamagata said in a statement published in the daily Tokyo Shimbun.
The Meteorological Agency report, however, did not say whether this year's El Nino could be worse than past ones.
